summary: Fortune's Paige Hagy argues that Gen Z, the first fully digital-native generation, watched the Hamas attack on Israel and the ensuing war unfold online, after growing up on a stream of disturbing images of historic events. The piece links this constant exposure to the generation's poor mental health, climate anxiety, purpose-driven workplace attitudes and financial despair. It closes by noting Gen Z's growing power and a warning that a hopeless young generation is not sustainable.
one_line: Gen Z, raised on online disturbing images, watched the Israel-Hamas war unfold on social media, shaping its mental health, work attitudes and finances.
key_facts: On Saturday, Hamas launched an unprecedented attack on Israel, resulting in the worst war the region has seen in 50 years; more than 1,500 people died on both sides in three days.
Gen Z, ages 11 to 26, has lived through the pandemic, the Jan. 6 insurrection, the war in Ukraine, and market crashes in 2008 and 2020.

A 2023 Edelman report found 46% of workers ages 18 to 26 are regularly so distraught over the news that they cannot function at work, versus 38% of millennials, 24% of Gen Xers and 19% of baby boomers and older.
A 2018 American Psychological Association report said 45% of young people report 'excellent' or 'very good' mental health, and the piece calls Gen Z's the worst of any generation.
A 2021 Pew Research report found nearly seven in 10 Gen Zers feel anxiety when viewing climate change content on social media.
July was the hottest month in over 100,000 years; Arizona had a monthlong heat wave with temperatures at or above 110 degrees every day.
Greta Thunberg, 20, spoke at the United Nations in 2019, telling world leaders 'You have stolen my dreams and my childhood with your empty words.'
By 2030, Gen Z will account for nearly one-third of the U.S. workforce, and they prioritize ESG in the workplace.
Roughly two-thirds of Gen Zers say they frequently speak about important societal issues at work, per the Edelman report.
A July Bankrate survey found roughly 60% of Gen Zers are more stressed about money this year than last, and 85% could not afford one month's expenses if they lost their job.
A Fidelity survey found 45% of 18- to 35-year-olds 'don't see a point in saving until things return to normal.'
In June 2020, teenage TikTok users and K-pop fans claimed to have sunk a Trump campaign rally by registering for thousands of tickets with no intention of attending.
After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, a then-19-year-old activist raised over $2 million in abortion funds by trolling Florida Rep. Matt Gaetz.
